roots.context: We have been learning how soap lifts oil and germs off our hands. Now we ask what a wash really does to the living things on our hands, and what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the turmeric test, plain water ran over the oily yellow and left it behind. A soap molecule holds oil and water at once, so the rinse carried the yellow away. Most germs leave your hands the same way, still alive, in the rinse water. A good wash moves germs to a place where they cannot reach your mouth.
deep_truth.habit: We talk about washing as a war that kills germs, because adverts do. A plain soap wash mostly moves microbes from one place to another, and that is enough to keep us well.
deep_truth.evidence: In the turmeric test, the yellow went down the drain with the soapy water. Plain soap kills very few bacteria, yet tests at home found it cleans hands as well as antibacterial soap that kills them.

three.who_am_i: Your skin is home to millions of microbes. A good wash leaves most of them where they live.
three.what_is_life: Bacteria sense what is around them and decide when to settle, swim or grow. On your hands, they live in the skin's oil.
three.what_is_this_world: In this world, oil and water stay apart by themselves. A soap molecule can hold on to both and join them.

roots.thread: Soap works because one molecule can hold two things that will not mix by themselves, oil and water. Your own cells are wrapped in the same kind of two-ended molecule, and so are the coats of some viruses. The water then carries the visitor microbes on, to the drain, the sewer and the soil, where many other microbes already live.

teachings.teaching: Uddalaka asks his son to put salt in water overnight. In the morning the salt cannot be seen, but every sip tastes salty. What is unseen can still be everywhere.
teachings.link: Germs and soap molecules are far too small to see. Like the salt, we know they are there by what they do: mould on bread touched by unwashed hands, and the fever numbers in Semmelweis's ward.

teachings.teaching: No living being should be killed, harmed or hurt, however small. Jain monks sweep the ground gently and filter their water so as to harm as few tiny creatures as they can.
teachings.link: A plain soap wash mostly moves microbes off your hands instead of killing them. It keeps us well while harming very few of them.

teachings.teaching: Among the five personal practices, the niyamas, the first is shaucha: cleanliness of the body and clarity of the mind.
teachings.link: Shaucha starts with keeping the body clean, and it needs care. In the turmeric test, the careful wash of every part of each hand was the one that worked.

science.text: Every cell is wrapped in a membrane of molecules with water-loving heads and oil-loving tails, built much like soap.
Plain soap removes most microbes from hands by lifting them off in the rinse water, and kills few of them.
Scientists estimate that about as many bacteria live on and in a person as there are human cells in their body.

other_view.view: Whether a germ is killed or moved matters less than keeping them from the next person. In hospitals, alcohol hand rubs that kill germs are used, because they are fast and work very well. Killing germs on purpose, with medicines and boiling, has saved millions of lives.

practice.title: A slow wash
practice.say: Let's wash our hands very slowly, and notice everything. Feel the water. Is it cool or warm? Rub on the soap and watch the foam grow. Listen to it. Rub every part of each finger, counting to twenty very slowly. Rinse, and watch the foam slide away down the drain. Now hold your wet hands still in the air. Feel them cool as they dry. Where is that water going now? Who will it meet next?
practice.kid: Wash your hands very slowly. Feel the water. Watch the foam. Count to twenty slowly. Rinse. Hold your hands still and feel them dry.

how_we_found_out.story: In the 1840s, most doctors in Europe thought childbed fever came from bad air, or from the weather, or from mothers' fear. Vienna's big hospital had two wards for mothers giving birth. In one, doctors and medical students helped the mothers. In the other, midwives did. More than twice as many mothers died in the doctors' ward. If bad air caused the fever, both wards should have suffered the same, because they were in the same hospital. A young doctor, Ignaz Semmelweis, looked for what was different. The doctors came to the mothers straight from cutting open dead bodies, and the midwives never did. In March 1847 his friend Jakob Kolletschka was cut by a student's knife during that work, and died of the same fever. So Semmelweis guessed that something from the dead bodies was carried on doctors' hands. From May 1847, everyone in his ward washed in chlorine water first. Deaths fell from about 18 in every 100 mothers in April to about 2 in June. Many doctors still refused to believe that their own hands carried illness. In 1879, Louis Pasteur found the microbes that cause childbed fever.
how_we_found_out.who: Ignaz Semmelweis, the midwives of Vienna's second maternity ward, and later Louis Pasteur
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Childbed fever came from bad air or the weather, and a doctor's hands could not carry illness. Comparing the two wards in one hospital showed the air was not the cause, and washing hands made the deaths fall.
